question: Which organism MOST commonly causes acute infective endocarditis with destruction of previously normal heart valves?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. S. aureus is the classic cause of acute IE — it is virulent enough to infect and destroy structurally normal valves, producing large friable vegetations with rapid clinical deterioration over days to weeks.

Incorrect. Viridans streptococci (e.g. S. sanguinis, S. mutans) typically cause subacute IE on previously damaged valves (e.g. rheumatic heart disease). They are less virulent and produce an indolent course over weeks to months.

Incorrect. Enterococci cause endocarditis (especially in elderly men with genitourinary instrumentation) but typically produce a subacute course rather than the fulminant destruction of normal valves seen with S. aureus.

Incorrect. HACEK organisms (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) cause subacute IE and are notable for being slow-growing, sometimes requiring extended culture incubation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the key distinction: Acute IE (S. aureus) → normal valves → rapid destruction. Subacute IE (viridans streptococci, enterococci, HACEK) → abnormal valves → indolent course.

S. aureus is the most virulent cause of IE — it can seed normal valves, produce large destructive vegetations, and cause acute clinical deterioration. In contrast, viridans streptococci typically colonise already-damaged valves in a subacute pattern.
